binders: Inherited notation: x is the spatial variable, t is time, and q is the evolving conserved state; the chapter introduces q : R × R → R^m in its one-dimensional setting (printed page 1, Introduction; printed pages 3–4, Section 1.1).
Inherited notation: f is the flux function of q (printed page 3, equation (1.8)).
The selected sentence contains no explicit quantified binders over fluxes, initial profiles, solutions, or times (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, page-spanning sentence).
hypotheses: The selected phenomenon concerns nonlinear conservation laws, with nonlinear dependence of f on q (printed page 4, opening paragraph and Section 1.1.2).
Smooth initial data are expressly included as data from which discontinuities can develop; no particular initial profile or smoothness class is specified (printed page 5, opening sentence).
conclusions: Discontinuities, discussed as including shock waves, can develop spontaneously during the evolution of nonlinear conservation laws even from smooth initial data (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, first paragraph).
Such discontinuities consequently require both mathematical and computational treatment (printed page 5, completion of the opening sentence).
At a discontinuity in q, equation (1.8) does not hold in the classical sense, while the integral conservation law (1.10) continues to hold (printed page 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph).
definitions_and_conventions: The one-dimensional differential conservation law is q_t(x,t) + ∂_x[f(q(x,t))] = 0 (printed page 3, equation (1.8)).
The flux is f(q); nonlinear conservation laws have flux nonlinear in the conserved state q (printed pages 3–4, Section 1.1 and its continuation).
The integral form is d/dt ∫_{x₁}^{x₂} q(x,t) dx = f(q(x₁,t)) − f(q(x₂,t)), stated for any two endpoints x₁ and x₂ (printed page 4, Section 1.1.1, equation (1.10)).
Subscripts t and x denote partial derivatives (printed page 1, paragraph following equation (1.1)).
Shock waves are given as examples of discontinuities; Section 1.1.2 supplies no separate formal definition of a shock (printed page 4, Section 1.1.2).
implicit_context: The claim occurs within the chapter's discussion of time-dependent hyperbolic conservation laws, presented first in one space dimension (printed page 1, Introduction; printed page 3, Section 1.1).

The smoothness qualification explains why deriving a classical differential equation from integral conservation does not cover all solutions of interest (printed page 4, Section 1.1.2, first paragraph).
The passage is an introductory qualitative assertion; detailed shock-wave theory is deferred to Chapter 11 (printed page 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph).

details: The phrase “can ... develop” asserts a possible phenomenon, rather than stating that every nonlinear flux and every smooth initial profile produces a discontinuity (printed page 5, opening sentence).

Reading the claim as requiring examples of such evolution is an analyst interpretation of its possibility language; the source supplies no explicit existential formula or witness here (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2).
The discontinuity develops from data initially described as smooth; a discontinuity already present in initial data would not alone express this claim (printed page 5, opening sentence).
The source provides no formation-time value, time bound, or rate of steepening in this passage (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2).
The asserted phenomenon is development of discontinuities in the solution, not merely an unspecified failure of differentiability (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, first paragraph).

Failure of the classical PDE at a discontinuity and continued validity of integral conservation are separately stated consequences of the solution framework (printed page 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph).

undebatable_constraints: Preserve the possibility language: the source does not assert shock formation for every nonlinear conservation law or every smooth initial datum (printed page 5, opening sentence).
Preserve smooth initial data and subsequent spontaneous development of discontinuities as essential features of the selected claim (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, page-spanning sentence).

Do not replace development of a discontinuity with only gradient growth or loss of classical regularity without further source justification (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2, references to discontinuities and shock waves).
Do not attribute a particular flux, profile, boundary condition, formation-time formula, or smoothness index to this passage; none is specified there (printed pages 4–5, Section 1.1.2).
Retain the distinction between the classical differential equation and integral conservation at discontinuities (printed page 5, Section 1.1.2, second paragraph).

contract_plain_english: Section 1.1.2 asserts that nonlinear conservation laws can develop discontinuities, including shock waves, spontaneously from smooth initial data (printed pages 4–5). This is a qualitative possibility claim without a specified flux, profile, regularity class, or formation time. The surrounding passage explains that obtaining the classical differential equation from integral conservation requires sufficient smoothness (printed page 4), and that at discontinuities the classical equation no longer holds in that sense while integral conservation continues to hold (printed page 5).
